purpose: Lorazepam is mainly used to relieve anxiety and help you feel calm. It is also used to help with sleep problems, to prevent or stop seizures, and sometimes to help you relax before a medical procedure. Doctors may also use it in the hospital to treat certain types of seizures.
how_it_works: Your brain has natural chemicals that help calm nervous activity, and lorazepam works by boosting one of those calming chemicals called GABA. Think of GABA like a brake pedal for your brain — lorazepam helps press that brake so your brain slows down its overactive signals. This is what makes you feel less anxious, more relaxed, and sometimes sleepy.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are feeling drowsy or sleepy, dizziness, and feeling unsteady or weak. Some people feel confused, have memory problems, or feel a little 'foggy.' You may also notice slowed breathing, especially at higher doses.
warnings: This medicine can be habit-forming, so it is important to take it exactly as your doctor prescribes and not to stop it suddenly without talking to your doctor first — stopping abruptly can cause serious withdrawal symptoms. Do not drink alcohol while taking lorazepam, as this can dangerously slow your breathing. It can also slow your breathing on its own, especially if you take too much. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, as it can harm the baby. Older adults should be extra careful because falls and confusion are more likely.
typical_dosing: For anxiety, the usual adult dose is 0.5 mg to 2 mg taken 2 to 3 times a day. For sleep, a common dose is 2 to 4 mg taken at bedtime. Your doctor will start you at the lowest dose that works for you. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, since doses vary depending on your condition and other health factors.
